title: 3-Read Friday #63: Teacher Growth, Tolerance Zones, and Maths Gems
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #63 of 3-Read Friday opens with Sam Sims's UCL CEPEO post asking why teachers in some schools keep improving well past the point where growth typically plateaus, which he answers using social capital theory's structural, cognitive, and relational dimensions. Carl Hendrick follows with a proposed 'tolerance zones' framework, borrowed from engineering, for calibrating retrieval practice difficulty so that it stays inside the 75-85% success-rate sweet spot that research suggests maximizes both learning and motivation. Jo Morgan closes the issue with her 187th 'Maths Gems' roundup of classroom resources, vocabulary tools, and AI-generated activities for maths teachers. Barton frames the issue around evidence-informed frameworks -- one for organizational learning, one for individual cognitive calibration -- bookended by a practical resource digest for maths specialists.
points: Sims's account of sustained teacher improvement rests on social capital theory's three dimensions -- structural (who talks to whom), cognitive (shared language for discussing practice), and relational (shared norms and trust) -- arguing prior research on peer effects only captured the structural piece.

Hendrick's tolerance-zone framework translates an engineering concept -- acceptable variance around a target spec -- into a concrete success-rate target (75-85%) for retrieval practice, with named failure zones above and below that threshold.

Sims's TIDE project plans to build the first validated measure of teacher workplace social capital and link it to value-added teacher data, aiming to test empirically what has so far been theoretical.

Barton's framing links all three items loosely under evidence-informed calibration: how schools calibrate collaboration, how teachers calibrate task difficulty, and how maths teachers calibrate their own resource banks.
quotes: Sam identifies the common theme in schools where teachers continue to improve (as opposed to plateauing after a few years).
He then suggests how leaders can use Social Capital Theory to implement this in their schools.
For retrieval practice to be effective, students must experience some success but also experience some challenge.
Carl dives into the research on Tolerance Zones to suggest an answer.

One for the maths geeks. The latest installment of Jo's regular offering of mathematical goodies contains some lovely vocab resources, activities created using AI, and some classic tasks from the late, great, Don Steward.
